stem: What is the minimum age to vote in a UK general election?
explanation: You must be 18 or over to vote in elections to the UK Parliament. In some elections in Scotland and Wales, people can vote at 16.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: In which year did the voting age for everyone become 18?
explanation: The voting age was lowered from 21 to 18 for men and women in 1969.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: In the 1830s and 1840s, the Chartists campaigned for every man to have the right to vote.
explanation: The Chartists were a group who campaigned for political reform, including votes for every man and secret ballots.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Which document signed in 1215 limited the power of the King and protected the rights of the people?
explanation: Magna Carta was signed in 1215. It was the first document to limit the King's power and state that the monarch must obey the law.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: The UK is a "constitutional monarchy". What does this mean?

options.label: The King makes all the laws
The King has limited power by law
The King is elected by the public
The King is also the Prime Minister

explanation: In a constitutional monarchy, the King or Queen is the Head of State but has limited power. The government and Parliament make the laws.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Which law, passed in 1689, confirmed that the King or Queen could not make laws without Parliament's agreement?
explanation: The Bill of Rights 1689 confirmed Parliament's power. It meant the King could not raise taxes or make laws without the consent of Parliament.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What was a major change made by the Reform Act of 1832?

options.label: It reduced the number of small voting areas
It gave all men over 18 the vote

explanation: The 1832 Reform Act increased the number of people who could vote. It also removed 'pocket boroughs', which were areas with very few voters.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: In which year did women in the UK get the same voting rights as men?
explanation: In 1918, some women got the vote, but they had to wait until 1928 for equal voting rights. Since 1928, all men and women over 21 could vote.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Who was the leader of the Suffragette movement in the early 20th century?
explanation: Emmeline Pankhurst led the Suffragettes. They were a group of women who campaigned strongly for women's right to vote in the early 1900s.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Who is responsible for keeping order during political debates in the House of Commons?
explanation: The Speaker is an MP chosen to be neutral. They stay independent of their party to ensure that all points of view are heard in debates.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What is a proposed new law called before it is passed by Parliament?
explanation: A proposed new law is called a Bill. It must be debated and passed by both the House of Commons and the House of Lords to become an Act.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Usually, what is the maximum amount of time between general elections in the UK?
explanation: General elections for the House of Commons are usually held every five years. The Prime Minister can sometimes choose to hold one earlier.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What name is given to the group of senior ministers who help the Prime Minister lead the country?
explanation: The Cabinet consists of about 20 senior ministers. Each minister is usually the head of a government department, such as the Home Office.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What is the main job of a Member of Parliament (MP) in the UK?

options.label: To represent people in their local area
To manage the local police force
To judge cases in a court

explanation: MPs represent every person in their local area, even those who did not vote for them. They handle problems and represent their area in Parliament.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Which TWO parts of the UK have their own devolved parliaments or assemblies?
explanation: Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland have devolved governments. These governments make decisions on local things like education and health.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Which TWO of these are the names of the two houses that make up the UK Parliament?
explanation: The UK Parliament has two parts: the House of Commons and the House of Lords. The Commons is elected, and the Lords is mostly appointed.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: The Habeas Corpus Act was passed in 1679. What does this law protect?

options.label: The right of the monarch to create new taxes
The right of a prisoner to be brought before a court
The right of all men over 21 to vote
The right of the government to close Parliament

explanation: This law ensures that no one can be held in prison unlawfully. Every prisoner has the right to go to court to see if their detention is legal.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What is the name of the voting system used for UK general elections?
explanation: The UK uses the 'First Past the Post' system. The candidate who gets the most votes in their local area (constituency) wins the seat in Parliament.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What happens if an MP dies or resigns before the next general election?

options.label: The seat remains empty until the next general election
The Prime Minister chooses a new representative
The local council votes for a replacement
A by-election is held in that area

explanation: A by-election is held to find a new representative for that specific area. This ensures the people living there still have a voice in Parliament.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Which group is formed by the second-largest party in the House of Commons?
explanation: The second-largest party is called the official Opposition. Their leader forms a 'Shadow Cabinet' to monitor and challenge government ministers.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Which TWO of these are true about civil servants in the UK?

options.label: They are elected by the public
They keep their jobs when the government changes
They are members of the House of Lords

explanation: Civil servants must be neutral and not take sides in politics. They work for the government and keep their jobs even when a new party is elected.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Most major government departments are led by a senior politician known as a Secretary of State.
explanation: A Secretary of State is a senior minister in the Cabinet. They are responsible for a specific area of work, such as health, education or defence.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What is the name of the daily record that lists everything said in Parliament?
explanation: Hansard is the official report of all debates in the House of Commons and the House of Lords. It can be read online or in libraries.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy
